title: On‑Prem Safety & Control‑Plane Talk Track + Competitive Gaps
content:
Purpose
Quick working draft: unify a concise talk track for sales/SEs when discussing 'customer‑managed control plane' with regulated buyers, capture common objections and recommended responses, and note areas where competitors are weak so we can emphasize differentiators. Not final — this is a scratchpad to iterate with legal and SRE.

Audience
- Sales reps, solutions engineers, CSMs prepping for security/compliance stakeholders
- Field product PMs building FAQ/help text

High‑level position (single sentence)
Redwood Private gives you the predictability and developer‑experience of a managed inference platform while letting your security and compliance teams retain full control over sensitive assets and networking — no telemetry in the control plane you don’t approve, clear upgrade policies, and integrated KMS/HSM options.

Key control‑plane concepts to communicate (short phrases for pitch)
- Customer‑owned control plane: control-plane components run in your VPC (or private datacenter); Redwood provides the control‑plane software package + support, not the hosted control plane.
- Zero‑trust connectivity model: agent-to-control‑plane (or control-plane-to-node) TLS mutual auth, explicit allowlists, and outbound-only management tunnels as an option.
- Data plane isolation: inference traffic and model artifacts stay on customer nodes; we never persist request payloads outside customer environment unless explicitly enabled.
- Ops handoff model: Redwood handles software patches and hotfix guidance, but any inbound changes require customer approval (configurable autopilot level).
- Audit visibility: full, customer‑accessible audit logs compatible with SIEM exports (Syslog, S3, Splunk).

Common buyer objections & suggested responses (concise)
1) "We can’t give you a control plane inside our network — too risky."
  - Response: "We deploy as software you own. The control plane runs in your account and under your IAM. Redwood’s support access is strictly role‑based and requires customer acceptance for elevated operations. We can demonstrate this in a security review and provide a short checklist for your security team."
2) "Who handles upgrades? Won’t Redwood push breaking changes?"
  - Response: "Upgrades are orchestrated by policy you set (manual, canary, scheduled windows). Breaking changes are handled via version pinning + canary rollout; we provide migration guides and rollback tooling. For regulated customers, we offer a change freeze/long‑term support lanes."
3) "Does the control plane phone home / send telemetry to Redwood?"
  - Response: "By default the control plane operates offline for telemetry. If customers want health phoning home to Redwood for SLA-backed monitoring, it’s an opt‑in channel with explicit consent, encrypted transport, and a scoped data schema. All diagnostic payloads are documented and can be filtered at source."
4) "How do we prove compliance to auditors?"
  - Response: "We provide an artifacts pack: architecture diagrams, data flow matrices, audit log samples, upgrade policies, and options to enable FIPS‑approved crypto + HSM integration. We also maintain a list of third‑party audits and can support an onsite review under NDA."
5) "What if Redwood is compromised? Could they access our models/data?"
  - Response: "Customer KMS keys live in your cloud account or HSM; model encryption keys never leave. Support access is role‑limited and requires customer authorization for sensitive operations. We can run a tabletop exercise to map blast radius and mitigations."

Competitive gaps & how to exploit them (notes for objection handling)
- Big cloud vendors (C1): Sell managed endpoints but often require tenant data in their control plane or restricted VPC peering. Pitch: Redwood's customer‑owned control plane avoids tenancy leakage and offers lighter egress/trust requirements for regulated data.
- Vendor X (self‑hosted runtime): Good at performance but poor at ops UX and upgrades. Pitch: Redwood pairs self‑hosted control with productized rollout, tracing hooks, and eval/regression tracking — lowers long‑term operational burden.
- Vendor Y (hosted with VPC connectors): Often black‑box telemetry and limited audit exports. Pitch: we provide SIEM‑friendly logs, customizable telemetry, and explicit export formats auditors expect.
- Open‑source stacks: attractive price but require engineering time. Pitch: Redwood reduces build‑vs‑buy risk by delivering hardened, opinionated defaults and documented compliance artifacts.

Technical guardrails customers ask for (and we should highlight)
- KMS/HSM integration patterns (BYOK), with short examples for AWS KMS, GCP Cloud HSM, Azure Key Vault.
- Network deployment templates: private subnet patterns, NAT/egress constraints, and optional jump/ bastion models.
- Upgrade policies: manual / scheduled / canary; show how rollbacks are implemented.
- Telemetry schema: list of fields we collect when enabled and where they flow (S3, REDWOOD-MON only if opt-in).
- Data residency controls: how artifact storage locations are chosen and enforced.

Suggested shortlines for slide decks (5–10 words each)
- "Keep your keys, keep your audit trails."
- "Managed inference without handing over the control plane."
- "Opt‑in health telemetry — you choose what leaves your VPC."
- "Version pinning and canary rollouts for regulated releases."

Open questions / legal & SRE review items (action items)
- Need exact language for "we never persist request payloads outside customer environment" — legal needs to review telemetry opt‑in/off wording.
- Obtain sample SOC2 control mapping for Private installs (we have hosted SOC2; map specific responsibilities for on‑prem).
- Finalize support access workflow: define ticket escalation that requires customer approval for RCE‑capable actions.
- Create a short terraform/ARM/helm example for 'control-plane-in-customer-vpc' and a corresponding checklist for network reviewers.
- Pricing implications for long‑term support lanes / security review assistance (one‑time + retainer?).

Field playbook snippets (how SEs should run discovery)
- Ask: "Where do your keys live today for database/app encryption?" -> ties to BYOK conversation.
- Ask: "What are your auditor’s top 3 concerns about platform access?" -> use answers to map to audit artifacts we provide.
- Demo script: show architecture diagram first (control plane in customer account) -> then audit artifacts -> then show how to toggle telemetry opt‑in and view an audit log sample.

Appendix: quick rebut phrasing for sticky objections
- "We don’t trust third‑party support access" -> "We don't require it; we run under your account and any support play is approved by your team. We can also do hands‑off guidance only."
- "We need FedRAMP" -> "Roadmap item; can discuss air‑gapped options and potential partner programs for PA/DP hosting — capture customer as strategic opportunity."

Next steps (who does what)
- Marco: draft a 1‑pager with the five demo slides and an audit artifacts checklist (due 2025-09-26).
- Sofia: legal: tune telemetry language and produce approved boilerplate (due 2025-10-03).
- Devon: infra: produce a small deploy repo + network checklist for SEs (due 2025-10-09).

Notes & references
- See confluence:PRIVATE-DEPLOY-ARCH-2025 for diagrams and current install matrix.
- Past field feedback: CS flagged telemetry opt‑out confusion 3x in last quarter; use this doc in next SE sync.

(End of draft — intentionally conversational and checklisty. Use this to build the formal FAQ and an SE one‑pager.)
